America in Summary

What the formal presidential record says—and cannot say—across 1789–2026

1,057 speeches · 4.2M words · 45 presidents · 1789 - April 2026

SynthesisChange, continuity, and uncertainty
Synthesis · Change, continuity, and uncertainty

What can presidential speech say about America in aggregate?

The chronology ends and six through-lines begin: agenda breadth, communication form, governing voice, adversaries, temporal appeal, and emotional register. Confirmatory, exploratory, and descriptive evidence remain visibly separate throughout. The present era is not uniquely doom-heavy; it is uniquely hype-heavy. Hype reaches 25.7 per 10,000 words versus 8.5 in the next-highest era, while doom is 8.9 versus a higher 9.3 in New Deal, world war & settlement.

America, in aggregate

The formal presidential record becomes more public-facing, more performed, less procedural, and more openly partisan. The category of enemy changes; presidents sell both tomorrow and yesterday; hope and doom move through the same historical shocks. These are changes in prepared presidential speech—not a single national personality.

01 · Voice

Who is addressed changes. How the address is delivered changes.

Who: Congress gives way to the general public. How: written messages give way to spoken, broadcast, and other performed forms. Read together across the same nine eras, the separate bars show a Congress-facing written record becoming more public and performed; the bridge below carries that chronology into the register view without treating audience or delivery as its cause.

Definition. A mutually exclusive primary-audience label assigned from the speech title and opening context.

Unit. share of corpus speeches.

Calculation.

  1. Read the title and opening context
  2. Assign one declared audience label
  3. Count labels within the displayed period

Example. An annual message addressed to Congress receives the Congress label even if newspapers later carried it to the public.

Limitation. It does not inventory indirect audiences, circulation, reception, or rebroadcasting.

01

WHO OR WHAT IS NAMED?

How the target mix changes

Five target types share one scale; highlight any line, then inspect six labeled changes in the mix.

Each era pools speaker-audited adversarial mentions · across the five lines, every supported era totals 100% · lines connect aggregates only

Highlight a line
All five target lines emphasized.
What each target category includes
Nation
Countries, governments, or national actors, such as the Soviet Union, Mexico, or Iran.
Group
Collective actors, factions, movements, or militant organizations, such as Democrats, Communists, or al Qaeda.
Person
Individuals or clearly referenced individuals, such as Saddam Hussein or “the Governor.”
Institution
Formal governing, legal, economic, or media bodies, such as Congress, the Supreme Court, or the United Nations.
Other
Residual ideologies, laws or policies, places, and abstractions, such as communism, the Taft–Hartley bill, or the Iron Curtain.

Each point pools speaker-audited adversarial entity mentions within one fixed reporting era; it is not an average of presidents or years. Repeated mentions count, and one paragraph can contribute more than one. Because the five shares total 100%, a rise in one category mechanically lowers at least one other. Era lengths, corpus density, and genre mix vary, and connecting lines guide the eye between aggregates without estimating values between them. Categories are frozen AI-assigned types; “Other” is a heterogeneous residual, not a single kind of enemy. A textual target is not a judgment that it was legitimate. The corpus currently ends in April 2026.

Evidence, limitations, and speaker-audited data
∑ Measure · Category of named adversary

Definition. The share of extracted adversarial entity mentions assigned to nation, group, person, institution, or other.

Unit. percent of adversarial mentions.

Calculation.

  1. Keep entity mentions with adversarial stance
  2. Assign the frozen entity type
  3. Count mentions by type within an era
  4. Divide by all adversarial entity mentions in that era

Example. If 60 of 100 adversarial entity mentions are nations, the nation category is 60%.

Limitation. Entity extraction and type labels can be wrong; the distribution excludes conflict wording without an extracted adversarial entity.

category adversarial mentions / all adversarial mentions

03 · Time

Presidents can sell tomorrow and yesterday at the same time

Compare the same two independent word families in two views: each president’s all-corpus record, or supported four-year rolling averages. A speech can invoke tomorrow and yesterday at the same time; this is not one scale running from past to future.

TOMORROW + YESTERDAY

Two temporal appeals, viewed together

Future-family and nostalgia-family matches per 10,000 marker words.

x = future-family matches per 10,000 marker words · y = nostalgia-family matches per 10,000 marker words · portraits use a uniform size · 3 records below the 5-speech precision floor use an amber halo

View

All nine eras emphasized.

∑ Measure · Temporal appeals by president and over time

Definition. Future and nostalgia matches per 10,000 marker words position each president and form two separate trailing four-year rolling averages of annual rates.

Unit. matches per 10,000 marker words.

Calculation.

  1. Pool every available corpus speech assigned to the president
  2. Count future and nostalgia families and divide each by marker words
  3. For the timeline, calculate each annual rate and average four consecutive years
  4. Require coverage in all four years and at least 10,000 total window words

Example. A president at 8 future and 5 nostalgia matches per 10,000 words sits at (8, 5); a timeline point averages the four annual rates ending in its displayed year.

Limitation. Each year receives equal weight in the rolling average even when its speech volume differs. Dictionary matches do not establish intent, feasibility, or historical accuracy; genre, quotations, other speakers, and uneven coverage can change the rates.

future rate = future/words × 10,000; nostalgia rate = nostalgia/words × 10,000

Source artifact. speech_markers.parquet + speeches.parquet.

Statistical status. descriptive.

Denominator / support. All 45 presidents aggregate every available corpus speech assigned to that document president. The time view averages four consecutive annual rates, plots each at the ending year, requires coverage in all four years, and applies a 10,000-word window floor. Both views divide exact future- and nostalgia-family matches by marker words.

Important caveat. These are unadjusted all-genre, document-owned transcript aggregates rather than speaker-audited claims. They are sensitive to genre, coverage, quotations, questions, and other speakers. Each year receives equal weight in the rolling average even when its speech volume differs. Dictionary matches cannot establish intent, feasibility, or historical accuracy.

LANGUAGE ACROSS THE BOUNDARY

Three ways presidential wording changes over time

Flip between a national naming shift, grouped stance words, and first-person language. These are separate lexical descriptions—not one scale of certainty, identity, or division.

National name: America overtakes the United States around the 1910 boundary.

Hover any line to highlight its full trajectory; click or tap to pin it, and press Escape to restore every line.

∑ Measure · Exact word and phrase uses per 10,000 words

Definition. A count divided by all words and scaled to a same-sized 10,000-word container.

Unit. mentions per 10,000 words.

Calculation.

  1. Count included words
  2. Count all words
  3. Divide and multiply by 10,000

Example. Five mentions in 10,000 words equals 5 per 10,000.

Limitation. Words can carry different meanings in context.

count / words × 10,000

Statistical status. descriptive.

Denominator / support. National naming keeps its governed centered five-year/20,000-word view; grouped stance and pronoun lines use centered seven-year windows above 10,000 words, which retain every 1789–2026 center year.

Important caveat. The grouped stance view combines explicit surface forms, not a certainty or extremity index. Definitions, downloads, and data-quality receipts →

National name1910 is the first start of five consecutive displayed windows with America above the United States.
Grouped stanceNecessity now includes the complete need word family and exact obligation phrases; commitment/intent joins will and shall to explicit speaker or administration pledge and intent phrases; absolute-emphasis wording remains separate. Solid lines and distinct decade symbols keep all five trajectories legible. Hover any line for a compact family definition, exact rate, year, and contributing presidents.
Personal voiceThe 2020s interrupt a century-long collective rise: I-family wording reaches its highest decade rate since the 1790s, but we still leads.
Inspect the 1910 naming rule and corpus examples

Exactly what is counted. The America family matches the whole words America, American, and Americans; the comparison family matches the exact phrase United States. Each count is divided by all words and expressed per 10,000.

Why 1910 qualifies. The chart sums counts and words inside a centered five-year window. A sustained crossover requires five consecutive displayed windows in which the America family is higher. 1910 is the first start that passes; 1909 fails.

What it may suggest—and cannot prove. The pattern may suggest a shift toward a shorter public name for the nation. It cannot prove a change in national identity: the family also captures adjectival and geographic uses such as “American commerce” and “Central America,” the corpus mixes genres, and the Miller Center collection is not exhaustive.

THREE TESTS OF A BROAD CLAIM

Is presidential rhetoric more divisive now?

More openly partisan, yes. More divisive in every broader sense, no. The three signals answer different questions, so they should not be combined into one index.

THE RESULT I STAND BEHIND

4.8×

Opposing-party attack in annual messages

The present-era rate is 4.8 times the Civil War & Reconstruction rate; the 95% speech-clustered bootstrap interval is 2.3–14.3×. The interval excludes one inside the one speech genre represented in every era.

A DESCRIPTIVE SHIFT, NOT A DIVISION SCORE

234 vs 329

First-person singular versus plural in the 2020s

I/me/my-family wording reaches its highest decade rate since the 1790s while we/us/our-family wording falls from its 2010s level. I stand behind those lexical rates; I would not call them evidence of divisiveness by themselves.

AN ANALOGY I WOULD CAVEAT

0.315

Nearest drift-detrended era: Civil War & Reconstruction

This is the present era’s closest relative match after removing adjacent-era drift, but 0.315 is modest absolute similarity. It is a historical rhyme, not evidence that the present is a rerun of the Civil War era.

The important limits: against the founding-era annual message, enemy naming is 1.09× (0.79–1.61×) and zero-sum framing is 1.76× (0.95–4.88×). Both intervals include one. The present era has only 10 annual messages, so all three ratio intervals carry the governed low-cluster caution.

Measures, provenance, and interpretation limits

Annual-message comparison. Paragraph shares from frozen combativeness annotations; 95% speech-clustered bootstrap ratios from combat/ratios.parquet. The interval component is sampling only.

Pronouns. spaCy-token counts from speech_stats.parquet, pooled within the 2020s and divided by all alphabetic tokens. The displayed chart uses centered five-year window totals.

Era analogy. Detrended cosine similarity from eras/era_similarity.parquet; “nearest” is a relative rank, not a closeness threshold, causal claim, or president-to-president match.

04 · Emotional register

Hope divided by doom

This is Hope/Doom—not Hype/Doom. It reports broad NRC hope matches for each narrow doom-family match in supported centered five-year windows. The log scale keeps low and high ratios legible; event lines orient the timeline, and tooltips retain both rates.

∑ Measure · Aggregate NRC hope count divided by aggregate doom-family count

Definition. The aggregate NRC hope count divided by the aggregate doom-family count in a centered five-year window.

Unit. hope matches per doom match.

Calculation.

  1. Sum NRC hope, doom, and words within the window
  2. Require at least 20,000 words
  3. Suppress a zero doom denominator
  4. Divide aggregate counts

Example. A value of 80 means eighty NRC hope matches for each doom-family match in that window.

Limitation. The two dictionaries differ greatly in breadth. A ratio can rise when hope increases or doom falls, so absolute rates remain in tooltips.

Σ NRC hope matches / Σ doom matches

Important caveat. Hope is a much broader dictionary than doom, so the ratio is not emotional balance or parity. Event lines do not identify causes.

Illustrated AI labeling methodology, complete taxonomy, prompts, agreement audit, and limitations →

Method note: most timelines are 5-year centered rolling rates weighted by word count, through April 2026, with points under 20,000 words omitted. The Tomorrow/Yesterday view is a trailing four-year average of annual rates with a 10,000-word window floor. The corpus before ~1790 is a handful of speeches, and one personal inaugural should not set a national trend line. Dots are per president per year: 46 years have more than one president speaking, and the corpus files a few famous pre-presidency speeches (Nixon's Checkers speech, Reagan's "A Time for Choosing") under the later president. This is the formal register only - major prepared addresses; rallies, debates, and social media are outside the corpus, so every trend here is presidents at their most prepared.
